items.title: Willie Hightower Interview, 1958-06-03
items.q: musicians around here just like, whatever you say Preston Jackson, I always think about him.

ctx.x: So many people did that all over the country.

We didn't have a dime. After 18 months, I didn't have a dime. Everything closed down after 1928. And musicians around here just like, whatever you say Preston Jackson, I always think about him. Because the boy was just in his primes, they're coming up, see. And he's got a wife, I don't know how many children he's got now. I don't know who they are. He had three or four of them. And the boy was just coming along, see, and it just upset everybody so you couldn't get nothing. There was musicians around just doing…
May's Sugar Factory out here in Commercial Avenue? No, I didn't know about it.

items.title: Preston Jackson Interview, 1973-09-07
items.q: Willie Hightower's wife was the financial secretary... she'd throw a few crumbs my way... Willie Hightower was sweet jazz. You ever hear his play? Yeah, on record. Sweet, yeah. He used to be sweet. Played the blues.

ctx.x: Well, as you grew on in years, did you hear any more music?

Oh yeah, I, in spite of me hearing this music, I used to say, the second line just like the rest of the kids. We used to try sometime way away from home, you know, out of the neighborhood. I remember I, I think it was about the 30th of May and some friends of mine and I, we, we came all the way down to French Bar Town and the boys got behind us and ran us all the way to the podgers and ramparts, you know. And so I always did love music. I used to do a lot of whistling. I still do. And so, but I didn't have no…
Where was he from? He's from New Orleans.
